title: Body Mass Index in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a screening tool used to assess weight status in children and adolescents, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters. Unlike adults, BMI in children is interpreted using age- and sex-specific growth charts due to rapid developmental changes. It helps identify potential underweight, healthy weight, overweight, or obesity.

sections.p: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a simple numerical measure of a person's weight in relation to their height. In paediatrics, BMI is a key screening tool for assessing nutritional status, but it does not directly measure body fat. For children and adolescents, BMI is calculated using the standard formula: weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². However, its interpretation differs significantly from adults.
b: BMI for children is plotted on age- and sex-specific growth charts (BMI-for-age percentiles) to determine weight status.
The same absolute BMI value can mean different things for children of different ages or sexes.
Adult BMI cut-offs (e.g., BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² for obesity) should never be applied to children.

sections.p: In paediatrics, BMI-for-age percentiles are used to classify weight status, reflecting how a child's BMI compares to that of other children of the same age and sex. This classification helps in identifying children at risk for health problems related to weight.
b: Underweight: BMI-for-age less than the 5th percentile.
Healthy weight: BMI-for-age between the 5th and 85th percentile.
Overweight: BMI-for-age between the 85th and 95th percentile.
Obesity: BMI-for-age equal to or greater than the 95th percentile.

sections.p: Abnormal BMI in children, whether low or high, is often multifactorial. In low-resource settings, both undernutrition and overnutrition can coexist, sometimes even within the same household.
b: Undernutrition (low BMI): Inadequate dietary intake (poverty, food insecurity), chronic infections (e.g., HIV, TB, malaria, intestinal parasites), malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic diarrhoea), genetic conditions, or chronic systemic diseases.

Overnutrition (high BMI): Increased caloric intake (processed foods, sugary drinks), decreased physical activity, genetic predisposition, endocrine disorders (e.g., hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome), certain medications (e.g., glucocorticoids), and psychosocial factors.
Glucocorticoids may increase BMI in children who are overweight when therapy is initiated, and these children are more likely to remain overweight.

sections.p: BMI itself is a measurement, not a presentation. However, the conditions leading to abnormal BMI can present with various signs and symptoms. A clinician must look beyond the number to the child's overall health.
b: Low BMI: Pallor, fatigue, recurrent infections, poor growth (stunting), muscle wasting, oedema (in severe protein-energy malnutrition).
High BMI: Shortness of breath on exertion, joint pain, early puberty, acanthosis nigricans, sleep apnoea, hypertension, signs of insulin resistance.
General examination should include blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and assessment for oedema or systemic disease.

sections.p: While BMI is a calculation, further investigations are crucial to understand the underlying causes of abnormal BMI and assess for complications. The choice of tests depends on the clinical context and available resources.

t.b: To calculate BMI and plot on growth charts. Accurate measurements are fundamental; use calibrated scales and stadiometers. If a stadiometer is unavailable, measure length for infants/toddlers lying down and height for older children standing against a wall with a measuring tape.

To screen for acute malnutrition, especially in children 6-59 months. A low MUAC indicates severe acute malnutrition, even if BMI is not yet critically low. This is a rapid, low-cost, and effective screening tool in low-resource settings.
To check for anaemia (common in undernutrition) or signs of chronic infection. A low haemoglobin may indicate iron deficiency, while elevated white cell count could suggest infection.

t.a: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
t.b: To identify intestinal parasitic infections (e.g., Ascaris, hookworm, Schistosoma) that contribute to malnutrition. This is a crucial and often available test in endemic areas.
To rule out HIV infection, a significant cause of chronic illness and malnutrition in many East African settings. Early diagnosis allows for antiretroviral therapy and nutritional support.

To investigate for hypothyroidism (can cause weight gain and poor growth) or hyperthyroidism (can cause weight loss). May not be readily available in all low-resource settings; clinical suspicion is key.
To screen for diabetes or insulin resistance in children with high BMI. Elevated levels indicate impaired glucose metabolism.
To assess for dyslipidaemia in children with high BMI, indicating increased cardiovascular risk. May not be routinely available.

sections.p: Abnormal BMI, particularly at the extremes, can be a marker for serious underlying conditions or lead to significant health complications. Clinicians must be vigilant for these signs.
b: Rapid, unexplained weight loss or gain: Suggests acute illness, severe malnutrition, or endocrine disturbance.
BMI-for-age below 3rd percentile or above 97th percentile: Indicates severe underweight or obesity requiring urgent evaluation.
Signs of severe acute malnutrition: Bilateral pitting oedema, severe wasting, lethargy, poor feeding.
Complications of obesity: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, sleep apnoea, fatty liver disease, orthopaedic problems (e.g., slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
Complications of undernutrition: Impaired immune function, developmental delay, micronutrient deficiencies, increased mortality from common infections.

sections.p: Management of abnormal BMI in children is complex and requires a holistic approach, addressing both the underlying cause and the consequences. It involves nutritional, medical, and often psychosocial interventions.
b: For undernutrition: Address underlying infections (e.g., deworming, antibiotics for bacterial infections, ART for HIV), provide therapeutic feeding (e.g., Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food - RUTF), micronutrient supplementation (e.g., Vitamin A, zinc, iron), and educate caregivers on appropriate feeding practices.

For overnutrition/obesity: Focus on lifestyle modifications including dietary changes (reducing sugary drinks, processed foods, increasing fruits/vegetables) and increasing physical activity. Involve the family in setting realistic goals.
Treat comorbidities: Manage hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidaemia as appropriate, often requiring specialist referral.
Psychosocial support: Address body image issues, bullying, and mental health concerns that can accompany abnormal weight status.

sections.p: Regular monitoring and sustained interventions are crucial for managing abnormal BMI in children. Prevention strategies should target early childhood and involve community-level interventions.
b: Regular growth monitoring: Plotting weight, height, and BMI-for-age on growth charts at every visit to track progress and identify trends.
Nutritional counselling: Ongoing education for families on healthy eating, portion control, and active lifestyles.
Community health programs: Promoting breastfeeding, diverse diets, hygiene, and physical activity from an early age.
Screening for complications: Regular blood pressure checks, glucose screening, and clinical assessment for other obesity-related comorbidities.
Early intervention: Addressing feeding difficulties or rapid weight gain/loss promptly to prevent severe outcomes.

sections.p: While BMI is a useful screening tool, it is often misunderstood or misapplied, leading to confusion with other measures of body composition or health status.
b: Weight-for-height Z-score: While both assess weight relative to height, BMI-for-age is generally preferred for older children and adolescents, while weight-for-height Z-score is commonly used for children under 5 years, particularly in malnutrition screening.

Body fat percentage: BMI is a proxy for body fat but does not directly measure it. Muscular children may have a high BMI without excess body fat, while some children with normal BMI may have high body fat (normal weight obesity).
Adult BMI categories: Applying adult BMI cut-offs to children is a common error and will misclassify many children due to their changing body composition and growth patterns.

sections.p: BMI, despite its utility, has limitations and can sometimes provide misleading information, especially in specific populations or clinical situations. Clinicians must interpret BMI in the context of the overall clinical picture.
b: Muscular children: Athletes or very muscular children may have a high BMI due to muscle mass, not excess fat, leading to a misclassification of overweight or obese.
Stunting: In children with chronic malnutrition and stunting (low height-for-age), BMI may appear normal even with significant wasting, as both weight and height are reduced proportionally.
Oedema: In children with severe acute malnutrition and oedema, BMI can be falsely elevated due to fluid retention, masking severe underlying wasting.
Genetic or ethnic variations: Growth patterns and body composition can vary across different populations, and standard growth charts may not perfectly capture these nuances for all children.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid, unexplained weight loss or gain
Signs of severe acute malnutrition (e.g., bilateral pitting oedema, severe wasting, lethargy)
New onset of symptoms like excessive thirst, frequent urination, shortness of breath, or joint pain in a child with abnormal BMI
Any signs of systemic illness accompanying abnormal weight status

faq.q: Why can't I use adult BMI cut-offs for children?
faq.a: Children's body composition changes significantly as they grow, and their BMI naturally varies with age and sex. Adult cut-offs would misclassify many healthy children as overweight or obese.

faq.q: Does a high BMI always mean a child is unhealthy?
faq.a: Not necessarily. While a high BMI-for-age percentile indicates increased risk, it's a screening tool. A very muscular child might have a high BMI but be healthy. Further assessment of body composition and overall health is needed.

faq.q: What if growth charts are not available in my clinic?
faq.a: While ideal, if charts are unavailable, focus on clinical assessment: observe for visible wasting or oedema, measure MUAC for children 6-59 months, and assess for signs of micronutrient deficiencies or comorbidities. Refer to a facility with charts if possible.
